blocks.heading: Trees
blocks.text: A tree is a connected, undirected graph with no cycles. Equivalently, it has exactly one simple path between every pair of vertices. Tree structures are useful for representing hierarchies.

blocks.heading: Tree properties
blocks.text:
A tree with n vertices has n − 1 edges. Removing any edge disconnects it. Adding an edge between two of its existing vertices creates a cycle.

Edges may be drawn straight or curved; the drawing does not determine whether a graph is a tree.

blocks.heading: Rooted and unrooted trees
blocks.text: An unrooted tree has no designated starting vertex. A rooted tree designates a root, which defines parent–child relationships. Its edges can be oriented away from the root to display that hierarchy.

blocks.heading: Unrooted tree
blocks.text: No vertex is designated as the root. The graph is connected and acyclic.

blocks.heading: Rooted tree
blocks.text: The top vertex is the root. Arrows show the hierarchy away from it.

blocks.heading: Nodes, edges, and family terms
blocks.text: A node is a vertex. An edge connects two vertices. The root has no parent. Every other node has exactly one parent, its neighbor toward the root. A node’s children are its immediate neighbors away from the root.

blocks.heading: Leaves and subtrees
blocks.text: A leaf has no children in a rooted tree. A subtree rooted at v consists of v and its descendants, together with the connecting edges. A single-node rooted tree has a root that is also a leaf.

blocks.heading: Depth, level, and height
blocks.text: A node’s depth is the number of edges from the root to that node. With the root at level 0, its level equals its depth. A rooted tree’s height is the greatest node depth—the longest root-to-leaf path measured in edges.

blocks.heading: Binary trees
blocks.text: In a binary tree, each node has at most two children, distinguished as left and right. A node may have no child, only a left child, only a right child, or both. The empty binary tree is also allowed in recursive definitions.

blocks.heading: Binary tree levels
blocks.text:
For a binary tree with root at level 0, level i contains at most 2<sup>i</sup> nodes. This bound is specific to binary trees, not all trees.

A tree of height h has levels 0 through h. Height and depth count edges, not the number of vertices on a path.

blocks.heading: Ternary and n-ary trees
blocks.text: A ternary tree has at most three children per node, often called left, middle, and right. An n-ary tree has at most n children per node. A general or generic tree may have any finite number of children; it has no fixed arity bound.

blocks.heading: Spanning trees
blocks.text: A spanning tree of a connected undirected graph is a subgraph that includes every vertex and is a tree. A disconnected graph has no spanning tree covering all its vertices. A connected graph may have several different spanning trees.

blocks.heading: Spanning tree properties
blocks.text:
Every spanning tree on n vertices has n − 1 edges. Remove an edge and it becomes disconnected. Add an edge between existing vertices and a cycle appears.

If the original connected graph has e edges, keeping a spanning tree removes e − n + 1 edges.
